newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Callebaut head sees chance of higher cocoa price.
newsitem.headline: Callebaut head sees chance of higher cocoa price.

text.p: Charles Gebhard, chairman of Swiss cocoa processor Callebaut said there could be some factors arguing for higher cocoa prices but the picture was complicated.
In an interview, he declined to give any price forecast but said he expected a slight deficit worldwide between the new crop and consumption in 1996/1997.
He noted said cocoa grindings in the 1996 calendar year looked higher, and said consumption, including in some central European countries and Russia appeared to be higher as well.
"Total consumption seems to be (running) at a two to three percent growth rate," he said. Grindings were up by about three percent so far this year, he said.
For entire world production, he said the current forecast was for 2.5 to 2.6 million tonnes for 1996/1997, with consumption expected at about 2.6 to 2.7 million tonnes.

"So there could be a slight deficit (in 1996/1997). But there are stocks, and stocks are at about a 1.2 million level," he said. The 1995/1996 production was about 2.7 million tonnes, and consumption about 2.6 million tonnes.
With respect to the Ivory Coast, he said it was still too early to have a definite forecast for the cocoa crop.

"Most probably we will have to wait another four weeks to find out what is really going to happen between October and December," he said. The Ivory Coast was hit by heavy rains. The rain may have hurt the crop, but there is a chance it could also have been beneficial.
Gebhard said the crop in the October to March period may be below upper estimates of 870,000 tonnes.
He said that estimates for the 1996/1997 crop ranged between 700,000 and 870,000 tonnes.
"Our forecast is certainly below 870,000, so that as a consequence, there might be some upward tendency short to medium term in the price," he said.

He said the current estimate for the upcoming season, including the midcrop, would be closer to one million tonnes. That would include a midcrop of between 200,000 and 250,000 tonnes, and a crop from October to March of between 750,000 to 800,000 tonnes, he said.
Total harvest in 1995/1996 was about 1.2 million tonnes.
Gebhard also cautioned that it was tricky trying to second-guess the market.

"In the past, we have gone through such periods, (such as) in 1992/93 and 1993/94 where all the cocoa traders were under the impression that prices should move up. They have moved up. But they have not gone as far as was expected," he said.
Cocoa currently is trading slightly below 1,000 stg per tonne. Gebhard noted that there had been expectations the market would move up slightly over 1,100 stg.

"People have expected the market would move up beyond 1,100 and we have seen it, and all of a sudden it went below 1,000 again. It is also a matter of what is happening in the market in terms of speculation," he said.
Traders in London have lately said that one firm was holding a large position in September cocoa and this was a factor which has made it more difficult to guage the market.
The position may be as large as 300,000 tonnes.
